impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that patent claims directed to humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity, reinstating a jury verdict that Eli Lilly willfully infringed Teva's headache patents covering anti-CGRP antibody treatments. The case involves Teva's Ajovy product and has significant implications for the scope of written-description and enablement requirements for biologic and antibody patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent holders' ability to obtain and enforce genus claims covering classes of biologics, including antibodies, where the specification discloses one species and references known methods for producing others.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar developers face heightened risk that broad antibody patent claims will survive validity challenges, potentially extending market exclusivity for biologic drugs.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a change from 'C2-C12-alkyl' in a provisional application to 'C1-C12-alkyl' in the non-provisional patent constituted correction of an obvious typographical error, thereby entitling the patent to the provisional's priority date and avoiding anticipation by Pfizer's intervening disclosure of nirmatrelvir (Paxlovid).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment invalidating Enanta's patent covering compounds used to inhibit coronavirus replication, holding that the change from C2 to C1 in the substituent definition was not an obvious typographical error and thus the patent could not claim priority from the earlier provisional. Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir anticipated the claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Protects companies like Pfizer from infringement claims where a competitor's patent priority depends on correcting errors in provisional applications that expand claim scope to cover the competitor's product.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent applicants face significant risk that even minor drafting errors in provisional applications may result in loss of priority date and patent invalidation, emphasizing the critical importance of provisional application accuracy.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's trade secret damages expert and damages model, and whether Ford was entitled to judgment as a matter of law on trade secret misappropriation liability under the DTSA and Michigan law.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court affirmed liability for Ford's misappropriation of Versata's automotive configuration software trade secrets and reversed the district court's breach of contract damages judgment, reinstating the jury award.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software developers and licensors benefit from the affirmation of trade secret misappropriation liability where a licensee develops competing software during the license term, and from the court's willingness to reconsider broader damages theories.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop in-house replacements for licensed software face heightened trade secret misappropriation risk, particularly when employees had access to the licensor's proprietary technology during the license period.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Insulet's Defend Trade Secrets Act claim for misappropriation of insulin patch pump trade secrets was time-barred under the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's denial of JMOL, holding that Insulet's DTSA trade secret misappropriation claim against EOFlow was barred by the statute of limitations because Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing suit. The court reversed the damages award and permanent injunction.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides clarity on the DTSA statute of limitations, benefiting companies accused of trade secret misappropriation where the plaintiff delayed in bringing suit despite having knowledge of the alleged misconduct.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly upon discovering or having reason to discover misappropriation; delay beyond three years from the date of discovery may result in complete loss of DTSA claims regardless of the merits.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied inter partes review estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar Valve from asserting invalidity grounds in district court litigation that were not raised in its IPR petition.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against Valve, finding insufficient evidence to estop one invalidity ground and that the court failed to adequately account for hindsight bias in estopping the other. The case provides important guidance on the evidentiary standard for determining what a 'skilled searcher conducting a diligent search reasonably could have been expected to discover.'
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from a narrower application of IPR estoppel, preserving their ability to raise invalidity defenses in district court that were not included in IPR petitions, particularly where prior art discovery is not straightforward.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face greater difficulty in using IPR estoppel to foreclose invalidity challenges in district court, potentially prolonging and complicating patent enforcement litigation.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and in rejecting VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory for a patent claiming methods for selecting processor cores based on processing speed.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit partially reversed the district court's summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's multicore processor patent against Intel, addressing the extraterritorial reach of U.S. patent law and the doctrine of equivalents. The court also addressed the propriety of striking damages expert theories for disclosure failures.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting infringement of method claims against global technology companies may benefit from a broader view of when domestic acts constitute infringement even when some steps occur abroad.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies with global operations face continued uncertainty about when foreign activities may give rise to U.S. patent infringement liability for method claims.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in using a single verdict form question covering infringement for all asserted patents and in its jury instruction on patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 at Alice step two.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgments and remanded for a new trial, holding that the single-question verdict form improperly bundled all asserted patents into one infringement finding. The court also vacated and remanded for further proceedings on the § 101 analysis for the '495 patent while affirming eligibility of other patents directed to wireless building automation systems.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement that verdict forms must allow juries to separately evaluate infringement for each asserted patent, preventing conflation of distinct patent claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased litigation costs and complexity from the requirement for patent-specific verdict questions, and risk retrials when verdict forms improperly combine multiple patents.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in its infringement and damages rulings.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents, all relating to non-uniform constellation designs for broadcast communications. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages, preserving a judgment against LG for willful infringement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Affirms that certain technology-specific improvements to digital communication standards can satisfy § 101, providing comfort to companies holding patents on communications technology innovations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies implementing industry standards face continued patent infringement exposure where standard-essential or standard-related patents survive eligibility challenges, potentially increasing licensing costs.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to a relay device for automated capture, processing, and sharing of farming operation data are patent-ineligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the case was exceptional warranting attorney fees.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming data collection patents were directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas under § 101 but vacated and remanded the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional under § 285, potentially opening the door for attorney fees. The patents claimed relay devices for tracking farming operations using GPS and bus connectors on farming equipment.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides additional authority for defendants challenging agricultural technology and IoT data-collection patents under § 101, and opens the possibility of recovering attorney fees in cases involving ineligible patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies holding patents on agricultural technology and data-collection systems face heightened § 101 invalidity risk, and the remand on exceptionality signals potential fee exposure for asserting such patents.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that has granted an exclusive license but retained the right to sue for infringement and other exclusionary rights has sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who retains the right to sue third parties for infringement and other meaningful exclusionary rights maintains sufficient constitutional standing to enforce its patents, even after granting an exclusive license. The case involved patents on warm-mix asphalt technology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners who license patents exclusively but retain enforcement rights are protected in their ability to bring infringement suits, providing greater flexibility in structuring licensing arrangements.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potential standing defense where the patent owner has retained meaningful exclusionary rights, even if an exclusive license has been granted to a third party.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify outside personal knowledge for purposes of summary judgment, and whether computer source code constitutes hearsay, in the context of an on-sale bar invalidity defense under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that a 30(b)(6) corporate witness may testify beyond personal knowledge at summary judgment and that computer source code describing commands is not hearsay. The ruling facilitated proof that a prior art device embodying all claim limitations was commercially sold before the critical date.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from expanded evidentiary tools for proving on-sale bar invalidity, including broader use of 30(b)(6) testimony and admissibility of source code as non-hearsay evidence.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face greater vulnerability to on-sale bar challenges when prior art products were sold commercially, as corporate representatives can testify about historical sales even without personal knowledge.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the jury's finding that asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law was supported by legally sufficient evidence, and whether ideas that are generally known can constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret claims involving cosmetic penile implant technology, finding insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law. The court also reversed on patent invalidity for incorrect inventorship, holding that generally known ideas cannot constitute an inventive contribution. The counterfeiting claim and damages were affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret cases benefit from heightened scrutiny of whether asserted trade secrets are genuinely protectable rather than generally known information in the relevant field.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret plaintiffs must demonstrate with legally sufficient evidence that each asserted trade secret derives independent economic value from not being generally known, or risk JMOL reversal even after a favorable jury verdict.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a non-party to patent infringement litigation may file an IPR petition on the filing deadline of the actual defendant, and whether the Board's obviousness determination was supported by substantial evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness finding against FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded, while declining to review the Board's denial of FedEx's motion to terminate the IPR. The case raises significant concerns about third parties filing IPR petitions as proxies for time-barred defendants, potentially circumventing the § 315(b) one-year filing deadline.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from the vacatur of the obviousness determination and the court's scrutiny of potential proxy IPR filings that may circumvent statutory time bars.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that rely on third-party IPR filings to challenge patents asserted against them face uncertainty about the viability of this strategy, though the court declined to categorically bar the practice.

impacts.caseName: Fortress Iron, LP v. Digger Specialties, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a court may correct patent inventorship under 35 U.S.C. § 256(b) when the patent holder cannot locate a missing coinventor, and whether patents are invalid for omission of a coinventor who cannot be found.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment invalidating patents for omission of a coinventor (a Chinese manufacturing partner's employee) whom the patent holder could not locate to add to the patent. The court declined to order inventorship correction under § 256(b) where the missing coinventor had not been contacted or consented. This highlights the risk of collaborative development with foreign partners without securing inventorship documentation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers gain a powerful invalidity defense when patent holders fail to name all coinventors, particularly in cases involving contributions from foreign manufacturing partners.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that collaborate with foreign manufacturers or partners on product development face significant risk of patent invalidation if coinventors cannot be located and added, emphasizing the need for robust inventor identification and documentation practices.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to pH measured at a standard temperature in the field, and whether Actelion was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding of no infringement of Actelion's epoprostenol (Veletri) patents by Mylan's generic ANDA product, holding that pH claim limitations must be interpreted at the standard temperature convention in the pharmaceutical field. The court also upheld the bar on Actelion's doctrine of equivalents argument. This facilitates generic entry for epoprostenol products.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies benefit from the court's rigorous claim construction requiring pH measurements at standard field conditions, which narrows the scope of pharmaceutical formulation patents and facilitates ANDA filings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies face narrower patent protection for formulation patents with pH-dependent limitations, as courts will apply standard measurement conventions that may exclude competitor products from literal infringement.
